questions.title: Ganglion supplying lacrimal gland secretomotor fibres
questions.question: A patient complains of dryness of eyes, there was decreased secretion of lacrimal glands, the most likely ganglion involved is?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The otic ganglion relays parasympathetic secretomotor fibres (via the glossopharyngeal nerve and lesser petrosal nerve) to the PAROTID gland, not the lacrimal gland.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ciliary ganglion relays parasympathetic fibres (via the oculomotor nerve) to the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle for pupillary constriction and accommodation — it does not supply the lacrimal gland.
explanations.C: Correct. The pterygopalatine ganglion is the parasympathetic relay station for lacrimal gland secretomotor fibres: preganglionic fibres travel in the facial nerve, its greater petrosal branch and the nerve of the pterygoid canal to synapse here, and postganglionic fibres reach the lacrimal gland via the zygomatic and lacrimal nerves. A lesion interrupting this pathway therefore reduces tear secretion and produces the dry-eye picture described. This is the reason the pterygopalatine ganglion is often called the "ganglion of hay fever" and the key relay tested for lacrimal (and nasal) gland dysfunction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superior cervical ganglion is a SYMPATHETIC ganglion; its fibres do reach the lacrimal gland as vasoconstrictor/hitch-hiking fibres, but the secretomotor (fluid-producing) supply — the one whose loss causes decreased tear secretion — is parasympathetic via the pterygopalatine ganglion.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the pterygopalatine ganglion as the parasympathetic relay for lacrimal gland secretomotor fibres, distinguishing it from the otic (parotid) and ciliary (pupil) ganglia.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Autonomic Ganglia of the Head > Pterygopalatine Ganglion

questions.title: Cervical plexus cutaneous branch crossing sternocleidomastoid
questions.question: What is the cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus that crosses over the sternocleidomastoid muscle?

explanations.A: Correct. The transverse (anterior) cutaneous nerve of the neck arises from the cervical plexus (C2-C3), turns around the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid at its midpoint, and runs HORIZONTALLY (transversely) forward across the muscle to supply the skin of the anterior triangle. This transverse course across the front of sternocleidomastoid is exactly what distinguishes it from the other cervical plexus cutaneous branches, which run in different directions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) ascends VERTICALLY over sternocleidomastoid toward the ear and angle of the mandible, rather than crossing it transversely.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4) descend over the clavicle to supply skin of the lower neck and upper chest/shoulder, not crossing transversely over sternocleidomastoid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lesser occipital nerve (C2) ascends along the POSTERIOR border of sternocleidomastoid to supply skin behind the ear, rather than crossing over the muscle's surface transversely.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the transverse cervical nerve as the cervical plexus cutaneous branch that crosses horizontally over sternocleidomastoid, distinguishing its course from the great auricular, supraclavicular and lesser occipital nerves.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Neck > Cervical Plexus Cutaneous Branches

questions.title: Embryological origin of a lateral cervical (branchial) fistula
questions.question: A 2-month-old male infant had a small pit at the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, with mucus dripping intermittently from the opening. The pit extended to the tonsillar fossa as a branchial fistula. Which of the following embryologic structure(s) is (are) involved in this anomaly?

options.D: Second pharyngeal pouch and cervical sinus

explanations.A: Incorrect. The second pharyngeal ARCH itself (which overgrows the lower arches to form the cervical sinus) gives rise to muscles and skeletal derivatives, not the epithelial-lined tract of a fistula.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A persisting second pharyngeal groove alone would form a lateral cervical CYST or a blind sinus opening only externally; a complete fistula opening both externally (on the neck) and internally (at the tonsillar fossa) requires the internal pouch component as well.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The third pharyngeal pouch forms the inferior parathyroid and thymus; it opens internally near the piriform fossa, not the tonsillar (palatine) fossa, so it does not match a tract ending at the tonsillar fossa.
explanations.D: Correct. A complete lateral cervical (branchial) fistula runs from an external opening along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid to an internal opening in the tonsillar fossa; it forms when the second pharyngeal POUCH (which gives the internal opening at the tonsillar/palatine fossa) persists together with the cervical SINUS (the remnant of the ectodermal grooves buried by the overgrowing second arch, giving the external opening). Because the internal opening is specifically at the tonsillar fossa, the SECOND pouch — not the third — is the pouch involved. The persistence of both the pouch and the cervical sinus is what makes it a through-and-through fistula rather than a blind cyst.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that a complete lateral cervical (branchial) fistula ending at the tonsillar fossa involves persistence of the second pharyngeal pouch together with the cervical sinus.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Embryology of Head and Neck > Pharyngeal Apparatus

questions.title: Structures whose fusion failure causes cleft lip
questions.question: A 2-day-old infant male has a noticeable gap in his upper lip. The diagnosis is a cleft lip. Failure of fusion of which of the following structures is the most likely cause of this anomaly?

options.A: Maxillary prominences/processes and the intermaxillary segment
options.C: Lateral nasal and medial nasal prominences/processes

explanations.A: Correct. The upper lip forms when the maxillary prominence of each side fuses with the intermaxillary segment (the merged medial nasal prominences), which contributes the philtrum and the four incisor-bearing part of the maxilla. Failure of the maxillary prominence to fuse with the intermaxillary segment leaves the characteristic gap of a (lateral) cleft lip. This maxillary-to-intermaxillary fusion is the specific step that closes the upper lip, which is why its failure is the classic embryological basis of cleft lip.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The two medial nasal prominences themselves MERGE (they do not simply "fuse" as separate structures) to form the intermaxillary segment; failure of the medial nasal prominences to merge with EACH OTHER would give a rare median cleft lip, not the typical lateral cleft lip described.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Failure of fusion between the lateral nasal and medial nasal prominences produces an oblique facial cleft (running toward the eye along the nasolacrimal groove), not a cleft of the upper lip.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Lateral prominences" is not the pair whose fusion closes the upper lip; the upper lip specifically requires the maxillary prominence to unite with the intermaxillary segment.

questions.learning_objective: State that cleft lip results from failure of fusion of the maxillary prominence with the intermaxillary segment (merged medial nasal prominences).
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Embryology of Head and Neck > Development of the Face

questions.title: Cortical area for general (somatic) sensation
questions.question: A 45-year-old man is presented to the clinic complaining of loss of general sensation on one side. Which of the following areas is most likely affected?

explanations.A: Correct. Brodmann areas 3, 1 and 2 form the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus, the cortical destination for general somatic sensation (touch, proprioception, pain and temperature discrimination) from the contralateral body half. A lesion here produces the contralateral loss of general sensation described. Its somatotopic "sensory homunculus" arrangement is the mirror of the primary motor cortex across the central sulcus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Area 22 (in the superior temporal gyrus) includes Wernicke's area, concerned with auditory association and language comprehension, not general somatic sensation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Area 17 is the primary VISUAL cortex; its lesion causes a visual field defect, not loss of general sensation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Areas 18 and 19 are visual ASSOCIATION cortex; their lesion disturbs visual interpretation, not general somatic sensation.

questions.learning_objective: Localise general somatic sensation to the primary somatosensory cortex (Brodmann areas 3, 1, 2) in the postcentral gyrus.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Cerebral Cortex > Functional Localisation

questions.title: Cortical area controlling bladder and bowel (paracentral lobule)
questions.question: A 55-year-old man is admitted to the emergency department with incontinence of urine and stool. Which of the following areas is most likely affected?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cuneus is the visual cortex region on the medial occipital lobe above the calcarine sulcus; its lesion affects vision, not sphincter control.
explanations.B: Correct. The paracentral lobule, on the medial surface of the hemisphere astride the central sulcus, contains the cortical representation of the lower limb and the higher-centre control of the bladder and rectal (anal) sphincters. A lesion here (classically a parasagittal/falx meningioma or an anterior cerebral artery infarct) therefore produces urinary and faecal incontinence, often with lower-limb weakness. This medial-surface, midline location is exactly why sphincter control is vulnerable to parasagittal lesions that spare the laterally placed limb and face areas.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The premotor area (area 6) is concerned with planning and coordinating movement sequences; its lesion causes apraxia-type deficits, not sphincter incontinence.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The parietal association area integrates sensory information for spatial awareness and body image; its lesion causes neglect or agnosia, not loss of sphincter control.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the paracentral lobule as the cortical region controlling the bladder and bowel sphincters (and lower-limb representation), whose lesion causes incontinence.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Cerebral Cortex > Functional Localisation

questions.title: Cortical area for motor speech (Broca's area)
questions.question: A 67-year-old man is presented to the clinic complaining of inability to talk. Which of the following areas is most likely affected?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The primary olfactory area (uncus/entorhinal region) processes the sense of smell; its lesion affects olfaction, not speech.
explanations.B: Correct. Broca's area (Brodmann areas 44 and 45 in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere) is the motor speech area that programmes the articulatory movements of speech. A lesion here produces an expressive (non-fluent, Broca's) aphasia — the patient understands language but cannot produce fluent speech, matching the "inability to talk" described. Its position just anterior to the motor cortex representation of the face and larynx is what links it to speech output specifically.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The premotor area (area 6) coordinates general movement planning; its lesion causes apraxia, not an isolated inability to talk.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The prefrontal area governs executive function, judgement and personality; its lesion changes behaviour and cognition rather than abolishing speech output.

questions.learning_objective: Localise motor (expressive) speech to Broca's area (areas 44, 45) in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Cerebral Cortex > Functional Localisation

questions.title: Cortical area for colour discrimination (visual association)
questions.question: A 72-year-old man is presented to the clinic complaining that he cannot discriminate the colors. Which of the following areas is most likely affected?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Areas 3, 1 and 2 are the primary somatosensory cortex for general body sensation, unrelated to colour vision.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Area 17 is the PRIMARY visual cortex, which detects basic visual input; a lesion here causes a field defect (hemianopia/scotoma), not a selective loss of colour discrimination.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Areas 41 and 42 are the primary AUDITORY cortex in the superior temporal gyrus, concerned with hearing, not colour.
explanations.D: Correct. Areas 18 and 19 are the visual ASSOCIATION cortex, where basic visual signals from area 17 are interpreted — including the higher-order processing of colour, form and movement. A lesion in this association cortex can impair colour discrimination (a form of visual agnosia) while basic sight is preserved, matching the isolated loss of colour discrimination described. This distinction between primary (area 17, raw detection) and association (areas 18/19, interpretation) cortex is exactly what the question is testing.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute higher-order colour discrimination to the visual association cortex (areas 18, 19), distinguishing it from the primary visual cortex (area 17).
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Cerebral Cortex > Functional Localisation

questions.title: Cortical area for skilled voluntary movement (primary motor)
questions.question: A 54-year-old woman working as a tailor presents to the clinic complaining that she has not been able to do her work for a few weeks. Which of the following areas is most likely affected?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Areas 40 (supramarginal) and 39 (angular gyrus) are parietal association areas; their lesion causes agnosias/apraxias and language-related deficits rather than a primary loss of the skilled hand movements a tailor depends on.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Area 28 (entorhinal cortex) is part of the limbic/olfactory memory system, unrelated to executing fine hand movements.
explanations.C: Correct. Brodmann area 4, the primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus, executes voluntary movement of the contralateral body, with a large cortical representation devoted to the hand and fingers. A lesion here weakens the precise, skilled finger movements a tailor requires, accounting for the inability to work. Its enormous "motor homunculus" hand area is exactly why fine manual dexterity is disproportionately affected by lesions of this region.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Areas 41 and 42 are the primary auditory cortex; their lesion affects hearing, not skilled hand movement.

questions.learning_objective: Localise execution of skilled voluntary (especially fine hand) movement to the primary motor cortex, Brodmann area 4 (precentral gyrus).
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Cerebral Cortex > Functional Localisation

questions.title: Ventricle between the pons and cerebellum
questions.question: Which ventricle lies between the pons and cerebellum?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lateral ventricles lie within the cerebral hemispheres, far from the pons and cerebellum.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The third ventricle is the midline cavity of the diencephalon, between the two thalami, not between the pons and cerebellum.
explanations.C: Correct. The fourth ventricle is the rhombencephalic (hindbrain) cavity, tent-shaped and situated between the pons and upper medulla in front (its floor, the rhomboid fossa) and the cerebellum behind (its roof). It therefore lies exactly between the pons and cerebellum as described, communicating above with the cerebral aqueduct and below with the central canal. Its cerebrospinal fluid escapes into the subarachnoid space through the median and lateral apertures in this roof region.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The "fifth ventricle" (cavum septi pellucidi) is a slit between the leaves of the septum pellucidum in the midline forebrain, not a hindbrain cavity.

questions.learning_objective: State that the fourth ventricle lies between the pons/medulla and the cerebellum.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Ventricular System > Fourth Ventricle

questions.title: Property of the pia mater
questions.question: Pia matter:

options.B: Is carried into all its sulci
options.C: Bridges over the various sulci on the surface of the brain
options.D: Its two layers enclose venous sinuses

explanations.A: Incorrect. The pia mater is a delicate, thin vascular membrane; it is the DURA mater that is the tough, fibrous outer meningeal layer.
explanations.B: Correct. The pia mater is the innermost meningeal layer, closely investing the brain surface and — unlike the arachnoid — dipping down into every sulcus and fissure, following the contours of the gyri and sulci exactly. This intimate adherence is why the pia cannot be stripped off the cortex and why subpial haemorrhage tracks along the brain surface. It is this feature that separates the pia (which enters all sulci) from the arachnoid (which bridges over them).
explanations.C: Incorrect. It is the ARACHNOID mater that bridges over the sulci, leaving the subarachnoid cisterns beneath it; the pia does the opposite by descending into the sulci.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is the DURA mater whose two layers (endosteal and meningeal) separate to enclose the dural venous sinuses, not the pia.

questions.learning_objective: State that the pia mater follows the brain surface into all its sulci, distinguishing it from the arachnoid (bridges sulci) and dura (tough, encloses sinuses).
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Meninges > Pia Mater

questions.title: Anatomical name of the cisterna magna
questions.question: Cisterna magna is applied to:

explanations.A: Correct. The cisterna magna is the anatomical name given to the cerebellomedullary cistern, the large subarachnoid space between the undersurface of the cerebellum and the posterior surface of the medulla oblongata. It receives cerebrospinal fluid from the fourth ventricle through the median aperture (foramen of Magendie) and is the site classically used for cisternal puncture. Its large size and accessible position below the cerebellum are what earn it the name "magna" (great cistern).
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cistern of the lateral fissure (cistern of the lateral sulcus) surrounds the middle cerebral artery in the Sylvian fissure, not the cisterna magna.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The interpeduncular cistern lies between the cerebral peduncles at the base of the midbrain, containing the circle of Willis structures, and is a separate cistern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pontine cistern lies anterior to the pons (containing the basilar artery), distinct from the cerebellomedullary cistern behind the medulla.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the cisterna magna as the cerebellomedullary cistern, between the cerebellum and medulla.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Subarachnoid Cisterns > Cisterna Magna

questions.title: Part of diencephalon attached to the posterior thalamus
questions.question: The part of the diencephalon attached to the posterior part of the thalamus:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The hypothalamus lies BELOW and anterior to the thalamus (forming the floor and lower walls of the third ventricle), not attached to its posterior part.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The epithalamus lies on the posterior ROOF region of the diencephalon (pineal gland, habenular nuclei), but the specific structures attached to the posterior thalamus that this question targets are the geniculate bodies of the metathalamus.
explanations.C: Correct. The metathalamus consists of the medial and lateral geniculate bodies, which project from the posterior (pulvinar) region of the thalamus. The lateral geniculate body is the visual relay and the medial geniculate body the auditory relay, so the metathalamus is literally the part of the diencephalon attached to the posterior part of the thalamus. Their posterior, inferolateral attachment to the pulvinar is exactly the relationship the question describes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The subthalamus lies BELOW the thalamus (containing the subthalamic nucleus, part of the basal ganglia motor circuitry), not attached to its posterior aspect.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the metathalamus (medial and lateral geniculate bodies) as the diencephalic part attached to the posterior thalamus.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Diencephalon > Metathalamus

questions.title: Part of the internal capsule carrying the optic radiation
questions.question: The part of the internal capsule that contains optic radiation is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The anterior limb (between the caudate head and lentiform nucleus) carries frontopontine fibres and the anterior thalamic radiation, not the optic radiation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The posterior limb (between the thalamus and lentiform nucleus) carries corticospinal, corticobulbar and sensory thalamocortical fibres; the optic radiation is beyond it, behind the lentiform nucleus.
explanations.C: Correct. The retrolenticular part of the internal capsule lies BEHIND the lentiform nucleus and carries the optic radiation (geniculocalcarine fibres) from the lateral geniculate body to the primary visual cortex, along with posterior thalamic radiation fibres. This is why a retrolenticular lesion produces a contralateral visual field defect. Its position behind the lentiform nucleus is exactly what distinguishes the retrolenticular part from the sublenticular part below it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The SUB-lenticular part (below the lentiform nucleus) carries the auditory radiation (to areas 41/42) and some optic-radiation fibres to the lower visual field, but the optic radiation is classically attributed to the RETROlenticular part in this teaching context.

questions.learning_objective: State that the optic radiation runs in the retrolenticular part of the internal capsule (behind the lentiform nucleus).
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Internal Capsule > Retrolenticular Part

questions.title: Fibres connecting corresponding areas of the two hemispheres
questions.question: Fibers connecting corresponding areas in the 2 cerebral hemispheres:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Projection fibres run vertically between the cortex and subcortical/spinal centres (e.g. the internal capsule), not between the two hemispheres.
explanations.B: Correct. The corpus callosum is the largest commissure of the brain, a broad plate of commissural fibres that connect corresponding (homologous) cortical areas of the two cerebral hemispheres across the midline. Commissural fibres by definition join matching regions on the two sides, and the corpus callosum carries the bulk of them. This interhemispheric linkage is why callosal lesions produce disconnection syndromes between the two sides of the brain.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cingulum is an ASSOCIATION bundle running within one hemisphere (in the cingulate gyrus), linking areas on the same side, not across the midline.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superior longitudinal fasciculus is also an ASSOCIATION bundle connecting frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital regions within the SAME hemisphere, not corresponding areas across hemispheres.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the corpus callosum as the commissural fibre bundle connecting corresponding areas of the two hemispheres, distinct from projection and association fibres.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Cerebral White Matter > Commissural Fibres

questions.title: Location of the lateral ventricles
questions.question: The lateral ventricles are located within which part of the brain?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cerebellum has no ventricle within it; the fourth ventricle lies in front of the cerebellum, not inside it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The brainstem contains the cerebral aqueduct (midbrain) and part of the fourth ventricle (pons/medulla), not the lateral ventricles.
explanations.C: Correct. Each lateral ventricle is a C-shaped cavity lying entirely within one cerebral hemisphere, with a body and anterior (frontal), posterior (occipital) and inferior (temporal) horns extending into the respective lobes. They communicate with the midline third ventricle through the interventricular foramina (of Monro). Their sweeping course through all the lobes of the hemisphere is exactly what makes them the ventricles of the cerebral hemispheres.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The diencephalon contains the THIRD ventricle in the midline, not the lateral ventricles (which sit within the hemispheres on each side).

questions.learning_objective: State that the lateral ventricles lie within the cerebral hemispheres, communicating with the third ventricle via the interventricular foramina.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Ventricular System > Lateral Ventricles

questions.title: Cranial nerve attached to the dorsal brainstem
questions.question: One of the following cranial nerves is attached to the posterior aspect of the brain stem:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The abducent nerve (CN VI) emerges from the ANTERIOR aspect of the brainstem, at the pontomedullary junction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The vagus nerve (CN X) emerges from the side (postolivary sulcus) of the medulla, not the dorsal surface.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The oculomotor nerve (CN III) emerges from the ANTERIOR aspect of the midbrain, in the interpeduncular fossa.
explanations.D: Correct. The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve to emerge from the POSTERIOR (dorsal) surface of the brainstem, appearing just below the inferior colliculi before curving around the midbrain. It is also the only cranial nerve whose fibres decussate before exiting, and the most slender cranial nerve. This unique dorsal exit is a favourite exam point and the reason the trochlear nerve is vulnerable in the ambient cistern as it wraps around the midbrain.

questions.learning_objective: State that the trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve emerging from the dorsal (posterior) surface of the brainstem.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Brainstem > Cranial Nerve Attachments

questions.title: Correct statement about the third ventricle
questions.question: The following statements concern the third ventricle, one of them is correct:

options.A: It is the cavity of the hindbrain
options.B: It communicates with the lateral ventricles through the cerebral aqueduct
options.C: It is continuous with the fourth ventricle through the interventricular foramen
options.D: The choroid plexus is located in the roof

explanations.A: Incorrect. The third ventricle is the cavity of the DIENCEPHALON (forebrain), not the hindbrain; the fourth ventricle is the hindbrain cavity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The third ventricle communicates with the LATERAL ventricles through the interventricular foramina (of Monro), not the cerebral aqueduct.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The third ventricle is continuous with the FOURTH ventricle through the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius), not the interventricular foramen — this option swaps the two connections.
explanations.D: Correct. The choroid plexus of the third ventricle lies in its ROOF, formed by the tela choroidea (a double fold of pia) invaginating the ependymal roof between the two thalami, with the plexus continuous through the interventricular foramina with that of the lateral ventricles. This roof location is the correct statement, while the other options misassign the ventricle's cavity of origin and its two communications. The plexus here contributes to cerebrospinal fluid production within the ventricular system.

questions.learning_objective: State that the third ventricle's choroid plexus lies in its roof, and correctly assign its communications (interventricular foramina to lateral ventricles, cerebral aqueduct to fourth ventricle).
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Ventricular System > Third Ventricle

questions.title: A region supplied by the middle cerebral artery
questions.question: The middle cerebral artery supplies one of the following parts:

options.B: The sublentiform part of internal capsule
options.C: Motor and sensory areas of the whole body
options.D: Medial half of orbital surface of cerebral hemisphere

explanations.A: Correct. The middle cerebral artery supplies most of the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere, including the auditory area (Brodmann areas 41 and 42) in the superior temporal gyrus. Because the auditory cortex sits on the lateral surface within the MCA territory, it is the region among the options that the MCA genuinely supplies. The MCA's broad lateral-surface distribution is exactly why its occlusion classically affects the face-and-arm motor/sensory cortex and cortical language and auditory areas.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The sublentiform (and retrolenticular) internal capsule is supplied mainly by the anterior choroidal artery and lenticulostriate branches, not attributed to the MCA as a whole in this option's sense.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The MCA supplies the motor and sensory areas for the FACE and UPPER limb (the lateral surface), whereas the LOWER limb representation on the medial surface is anterior cerebral artery territory — so it does not supply the "whole body" representation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The medial half of the orbital (inferior frontal) surface is supplied by the ANTERIOR cerebral artery, not the middle cerebral artery.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that the middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral surface of the hemisphere including the auditory area, distinguishing MCA from anterior cerebral artery territory.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Cerebral Vasculature > Middle Cerebral Artery

questions.title: Structure forming the posterior surface of the midbrain
questions.question: The posterior surface of midbrain is represented by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The fourth ventricle belongs to the pons and medulla (hindbrain); the midbrain's cavity is the narrow cerebral aqueduct, not part of the fourth ventricle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. As with option A, the fourth ventricle is a hindbrain cavity, not the posterior surface of the midbrain.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cerebral peduncles (crura cerebri) form the ANTERIOR (ventral) surface of the midbrain, not the posterior surface.
explanations.D: Correct. The posterior (dorsal) surface of the midbrain is the tectum, formed by the corpora quadrigemina — the paired superior and inferior colliculi. The superior colliculi are visual reflex centres and the inferior colliculi auditory relay centres, and the trochlear nerves emerge just below the inferior colliculi. This dorsal tectal plate of four colliculi is exactly what "corpora quadrigemina" (four bodies) names.

questions.learning_objective: State that the corpora quadrigemina (tectum, superior and inferior colliculi) form the posterior surface of the midbrain, the cerebral peduncles forming the anterior surface.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Anatomy > Brainstem > Midbrain

questions.title: Fissure separating flocculonodular from posterior lobe
questions.question: The fissure that separates the flocculonodular lobe from posterior lobe of the cerebellum:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The primary fissure separates the ANTERIOR lobe from the POSTERIOR lobe of the cerebellum, not the flocculonodular lobe.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The horizontal fissure runs around the cerebellar margin dividing the superior and inferior surfaces of the posterior lobe; it does not demarcate the flocculonodular lobe.
explanations.C: Correct. The posterolateral fissure is the fissure that separates the flocculonodular lobe (the phylogenetically oldest, vestibular part of the cerebellum) from the posterior lobe. It is the first cerebellar fissure to appear in development, which is consistent with the flocculonodular lobe being the oldest part. Recognising this fissure is what allows the three-lobe division of the cerebellum (anterior, posterior, flocculonodular) to be defined.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Lateral fissure" refers to the Sylvian fissure of the cerebrum, not a cerebellar fissure.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the posterolateral fissure as separating the flocculonodular lobe from the posterior lobe of the cerebellum.

questions.title: Course of the superficial middle cerebral vein
questions.question: Concerning the superficial middle cerebral vein choose one best answer:

options.A: It lies in the posterior ramus of the lateral sulcus
options.B: It receives the majority of inferior cerebral veins of the medial surface
options.D: Ends in the superior sagittal sinus

explanations.A: Correct. The superficial middle cerebral vein runs along the posterior ramus of the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure), following it over the lateral surface of the hemisphere as it drains the areas around the fissure. From there it passes forward and downward to end in the cavernous sinus (and communicates with the transverse/superior sagittal sinuses via the superior and inferior anastomotic veins). Its position running within the lateral sulcus is the defining anatomical fact this option captures.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Drainage of the inferior/medial surface veins is not the role of the superficial middle cerebral vein; it drains the cortex adjacent to the lateral sulcus on the lateral surface.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superficial middle cerebral vein drains chiefly into the CAVERNOUS sinus (via the sphenoparietal sinus), not directly into the transverse sinus — the transverse sinus is reached indirectly through the inferior anastomotic vein (of Labbe).
explanations.D: Incorrect. It does not end in the superior sagittal sinus; that superior connection is made indirectly through the superior anastomotic vein (of Trolard).

questions.learning_objective: State that the superficial middle cerebral vein runs in the (posterior ramus of the) lateral sulcus and drains chiefly to the cavernous sinus.

questions.title: Arterial supply of the lumbar enlargement of the spinal cord
questions.question: The arterial supply of the lumbar enlargement of the spinal cord:

explanations.A: Correct. The arteria radicularis magna (great anterior radicular artery, or artery of Adamkiewicz) is the dominant segmental feeder that reinforces the anterior spinal artery in the lower thoracic and lumbar region, and is the principal blood supply to the lumbar (lumbosacral) enlargement of the spinal cord. Because this single large radicular artery supplies so much of the lower cord, its interruption (e.g. during aortic surgery) risks infarction of the lumbar enlargement and anterior spinal artery syndrome. This critical, size-based dominance over the lower cord is exactly why it is the specific answer rather than the anterior spinal artery in general.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The anterior spinal artery runs the whole length of the cord but is thin and inadequate on its own in the lower regions; it depends on the arteria radicularis magna to reinforce it there — so the artery specifically supplying the lumbar enlargement is the radicularis magna.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The posterior spinal arteries supply only the posterior (dorsal) columns and posterior third of the cord, not the bulk of the lumbar enlargement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The basilar artery supplies the brainstem and cerebellum, not the spinal cord's lumbar enlargement.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the arteria radicularis magna (artery of Adamkiewicz) as the dominant arterial supply to the lumbar enlargement of the spinal cord.
